newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says would defend currency against China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says would defend currency against China.

text.p: Finance Minister Paul Chiu said on Tuesday the government again would defend Taiwan's currency and financial stability if rival China were to mount intimidating war games like those staged in 1995 and early 1996.

"Judging from the military exercises conducted by mainland China in the latter part of last year and in March this year you can see the (Taiwan) government is very determined here to maintain financial stability, especially to maintain exchange rate stability," Chiu told Reuters in an interview.

Chiu, then a central bank vice governor, helped to oversee massive intervention to defend a skittish Taiwan dollar at T$27.5 to the U.S. dollar as China mounted waves of war games in the Taiwan strait and lobbed unarmed missiles into waters near its main ports ahead of Taiwan's March presidential election.
"I think we would still do these kinds of things if a similar kind of military exercise conducted by mainland China happened once again," Chiu said.
Beijing acknowledged the manoeuvres were to cool sentiment for anything but Taiwan's reunification with the mainland.
Taipei officially espouses reunification, but Beijing regularly accuses President Lee Teng-hui's government of acting to secure Taiwan's independence as a sovereign state.
Beijing has vowed to use force to thwart independence.

China began a spate of military exercises near Taiwan soon after Lee made a private but high-profile visit to the United States in June 1995, a journey that Beijing assailed as proof of what it called Lee's pro-independence policies.
Lee maintains there has been no change in Taiwan's position on reunification, saying it is a national goal but cannot happen until China adopts a pluralist political system.
China has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since the Chinese Nationalist government, toppled by the communists in a civil war, fled into exile on the island in 1949.
